pages.text: It appeared overnight on the wall of the maintenance storage area on the east side of the estate. A weaver bird, life-sized, in precise detail: the yellow of the breast, the chestnut of the head, the geometry of the half-built nest hanging from an invisible branch. It was painted directly onto the concrete. It was extraordinary.

image.note: Illustration: the weaver bird mural on a grey concrete wall, vibrant and detailed, morning light catching it

pages.text: Hanan found it on the way to school and was late because she stood looking at it for six minutes. She told everyone. By the afternoon, most of the estate children had visited the wall. By the following morning, there was a second painting two walls away: a hammerkop standing in shallow water, reflected.

The estate management committee posted a notice. Unauthorised painting of estate property is prohibited. The artist or artists are requested to come forward. Repeated unauthorised painting will result in removal of all works at the artist's expense.

'The management wants to remove them,' Nosa said. 'The management is wrong,' Hanan said, which was not something she said often about adults, but she had now spent forty-five minutes looking at the weaver bird and had formed a strong opinion.

image.note: Illustration: five estate children in a circle near the weaver bird mural, talking quietly

pages.text: 'If we find the artist before the management does,' Chinasa said, 'maybe we can get the paintings protected first. Like the hut plaque.' Everyone looked at her. 'What?' she said. 'It worked before.'

The investigation lasted four days. They ruled out: the new girl Zara, who had seen the paintings but had not painted them and was slightly offended at being asked; an older boy named Femi who painted but only on paper; and a secondary school student who lived in the estate and had art supplies but had been visiting family in Enugu all week.

On the fourth day, Ini said: 'The paintings are all near the maintenance areas. On walls that the gardeners and maintenance workers walk past every day.' Nobody said anything. 'The paintings are of Nigerian birds,' Ini said. 'All of them. Very accurate ones.' Still nothing. 'Vitalis has a bird book,' Ini said. 'I have seen it in his pocket.'

By the second morning there were two paintings, and by the third the whole estate was talking. Groups of children detoured on their way to school to stand in front of the weaver bird and the hammerkop, and one or two grown-ups, pretending they were only passing, slowed to look as well. Someone had done this in the dark, quickly and quietly, and vanished, and the mystery of it was almost as good as the paintings themselves. Almost. The paintings were very good.

Then came the notice, in the flat grey language that notices are always written in, and the mood changed. Unauthorised painting of estate property is prohibited. The word prohibited sat on the board like a closed door. Hanan read it three times and felt something she was not used to feeling about a grown-up decision, which was that it was simply, plainly wrong. The birds were the best thing that had happened to the estate walls in living memory, and the management wanted them gone.

Vitalis was the estate head gardener and had worked on the estate for nine years. He was a quiet man who knew the name of every plant on the estate, including the ones the estate had not intended to grow, and who fixed irrigation problems at inconvenient hours without being asked, because the timing of a plant's water needs did not align itself with office hours.

image.note: Illustration: Vitalis kneeling beside a flower bed, a small bird book visible in his breast pocket

pages.text: Ini spoke to him directly, which was her approach to most situations. 'Are you painting the murals?' Vitalis looked at her for a moment. 'Yes,' he said. 'The management wants to remove them,' Ini said. 'I know,' Vitalis said. 'I saw the notice.' 'Why do you paint on the walls instead of canvas?' Ini asked. 'Canvas costs money,' Vitalis said. 'The walls are there. And I thought no one was looking at them.'
'We are looking at them,' Ini said. 'I can see that now,' said Vitalis. He did not look displeased about it.

Ini reported back to the group. The group reported to their parents that evening. This was faster than the usual route because Chinasa's mother asked one direct question at dinner, received one direct answer, and had photographed all six murals herself before eight o'clock. She emailed the images to the estate management company's regional director, who had not seen them, and whose reply was a question rather than a statement.

The investigation was thorough, because Ini insisted it be thorough, and Ini was usually right about such things. They ruled out the obvious suspects one by one, the way you are supposed to, and the ruling-out took four days and produced several apologies. And then Ini, who had been quiet through all of it, mentioned the two facts she had been holding: that every painting stood near the maintenance areas, on walls the gardeners passed each day, and that Vitalis carried a small, well-thumbed book of Nigerian birds in his breast pocket.

Nobody had suspected Vitalis, because nobody really looked at Vitalis. He was the man who made the flowers grow and fixed the pipes at odd hours and knew the name of every plant, wanted and unwanted, on the estate. He was part of the background, like the walls themselves. That, Ini thought, was probably why he had believed no one would notice a few birds appearing on those walls. He had spent nine years being not quite noticed. He had assumed his paintings would be the same.

The regional director visited the following week. She stood in front of the weaver bird for a long time. Then she stood in front of the hammerkop. Then she walked to the far maintenance yard where Vitalis had painted a pair of sacred ibis in flight and a long-tailed paradise whydah in full breeding plumage, which required a wall three metres high to accommodate.

image.note: Illustration: the regional director and Vitalis standing before the paradise whydah mural, both looking up

pages.text: 'Did you study art?' she asked. 'No,' Vitalis said. 'I studied what the birds look like.' 'These are very good,' she said. He said thank you in the way of someone who does not receive this kind of comment often and is not entirely sure how to receive it.

The management committee agreed to protect all existing murals and to permit Vitalis to continue painting on designated walls. A small sign was added to the weaver bird wall: Tafiya Estate Bird Series, by Vitalis. No surname, at his request. He said the work should be about the birds.

Hanan visited the weaver bird the following morning at the same time she had found it the first day. The morning light was the same. The bird was the same. She stood there for six minutes again, because six minutes was apparently the right amount of time for a weaver bird, and then went to school.
